site.name: lumen-research
site.summary: Lumen Research — research assistant (local demo) Fictional research-assistant chat product. Local fixture for UXBench. Open `index.html` directly. Page `index.html` — Research thread Three-column layout: left rail for thread history, center conversation, right rail for Sources. Center column: - Conversation styled with serif body type. Each assistant turn renders inline citations as small chips (`[1]`, `[2]` …). Hovering a citation highlights and scrolls the matching source on the right; clicking jumps to it. - Embedded tables and lists are styled with the rest of the conversation.

run_plan.goal: Explore and critique the UX of the Lumen Research chatbot interface, focusing on the primary research-assistant flow, thread navigation, citation interactions, and mobile responsiveness.
run_plan.summary: The exploration will proceed in phases: first, validate the main chat interaction and citation functionality on desktop. Then, test thread navigation and export features. Next, check mobile responsiveness and re-verify key interactions. Finally, explore secondary threads and edge cases like new thread creation and mode switching.
assumptions: The site has only one HTML page (index.html) with a multi-thread chat interface.
Citation chips ([1], [2], etc.) link to sources in the right rail.
Thread navigation is via the left rail links.
risk_hotspots: Citation chip interactions (hover/click) for source navigation
Small tap targets on mobile (left rail links)

phases.title: Main Chat Interaction & Citations
phases.objective: Validate the core chat experience and citation linking.
key_checks: Click a citation chip (e.g., [1], [2]) to verify it jumps to the correct source in the right rail.
Hover a citation chip to check if it highlights the matching source (scroll behavior).
Interact with the text input field (ask a follow-up) and submit a query (using the 'Ask' button).
exit_criteria: Citation linking (click/hover) works, and text input/submit is functional.

phases.title: Thread Navigation & Export
phases.objective: Test thread switching and export/share features.
key_checks: Click a different thread in the left rail (e.g., 'EV battery recycling policy in Norway') to switch conversations.
Click 'Export as PDF' to verify the export functionality (check for download or confirmation).
Click 'Share thread' to test the sharing feature (check for modal or link generation).
exit_criteria: Thread switching works, and export/share features are responsive.

phases.title: Mobile Responsiveness (Desktop → Mobile)
phases.objective: Validate the interface on mobile viewport, focusing on tap targets and layout.
key_checks: Switch to mobile viewport and recheck citation chip interactions (click/hover).
Test thread navigation on mobile (tap left rail links) — check for small tap target issues (per layout warnings).
Verify text input and button sizes on mobile (ensure they're touch-friendly).
exit_criteria: Key interactions work on mobile, and tap targets are usable (or issues are documented).

phases.title: Mode Switching & Secondary Threads
phases.objective: Explore mode dropdowns and secondary thread workflows.
key_checks: Interact with the mode dropdown (e.g., 'Balanced' → 'Quick scan') to switch modes and check UI updates.
Click '+ New thread' to create a new conversation and verify thread creation flow.
Switch back to the original thread ('Deep work scheduling literature') to confirm thread management.
exit_criteria: Mode switching updates the UI, and new thread creation/management works.

phases.title: Edge Cases & Accessibility Checks
phases.objective: Test edge cases and accessibility-related elements (unlabeled selects, small targets).
key_checks: Interact with unlabeled select elements (e.g., mode dropdowns) to check for usability (aria-labels or tooltips).
Check the 'Sort: Relevance' dropdown in the sources rail to verify sorting options.
Test the 'New thread' button on mobile to check tap target size (per layout warnings).
exit_criteria: Unlabeled selects are usable (or issues are documented), and sorting works.

coverage_targets.pages: Visit and interact with all known pages (only index.html, so fully explore it).
coverage_targets.features: Exercise all visible controls: text input, citation chips, thread links, export/share, mode dropdowns, source sorting, and new thread creation.
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat critical checks (citation links, thread navigation, text input) on mobile viewport.

notes: Since there's only one HTML page, focus on different states and interactions within index.html. Document any layout warnings (small tap targets, unlabeled selects) as part of the critique.

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertnes

observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertnes

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertnes

What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertnes

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." How do I pre-register this study on OSF? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or stron

observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." How do I pre-register this study on OSF? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Wa

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." How do I pre-register this study on OSF? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Wa

What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertness occurring after 14:00."
